source.title: TinySQL: A Progressive Text-to-SQL Dataset for Mechanistic Interpretability Research
source.authors: P. Quirke; Clement Neo; Abir Harrasse; Dhruv Nathawani; Luke Marks; Amirali Abdullah

record.tranche_reason: The paper does not measure whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs. It notes overlap among attention heads involved in different SQL functions, but presents polysemanticity only as one possible explanation, not as a test of the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's SAE and circuit analyses concern SQL-generation components, not neuron-level responses to unrelated inputs. Its qualitative head-overlap observation is recorded as a related finding under fits_no_version. Background statements about features and SAEs are not study results.
record.test_reason: The paper builds a text-to-SQL interpretability testbed and identifies circuits with EAP, SAEs, ablation and logit lens. It never measures whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs. Its one mention of polysemanticity (Appendix J) is a speculative explanation for attention-head overlap, and the authors offer an alternative explanation alongside it. So it neither tests nor uses the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that TinySQL is a useful testbed and that SQL generation is compositional: intent first, schema grounding later. They find circuit results distributed, fragmented in larger models, and sensitive to ablation method and prompt. The polysemantic-heads remark is a minor appendix speculation with an offered alternative, not a conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies SQL-generation circuits using EAP, SAEs, ablation, and logit-lens analysis; it does not reproduce the original neuron-response method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that circuit and activation-patching results vary with method and ablation strategy, and that activation-patching results differ across prompts. It does not test whether those choices alter neuron-polysemanticity judgments.

fits_no_version.finding: In BM1 (TinyStories-33M fine-tuned), SAE-derived important attention heads for table-name and field/ORDER BY tokens largely coincide, e.g. Layer 0 heads [1,10,8,14] (Tables 10–12). This is described qualitatively as high overlap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The same attention heads serve multiple related SQL sub-functions. This is consistent with either polysemantic heads or a shared prompt-selection mechanism, and the study does not distinguish the two.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2025)
record.problems: The finding relevant to polysemanticity is qualitative and unquantified, and concerns attention heads rather than individual neurons. The authors themselves offer an alternative explanation for the overlap.
record.rows_left_out: No other results directly bear on the claim versions; the paper's circuit-recovery accuracies and logit-lens results measure SQL-task performance or generation stages, not neuron polysemanticity.

untested.parts: Prevalence of polysemantic MLP neurons in language models, and its variation by layer, is not measured.
No test of superposition as a cause.
No test of polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
No comparison of polysemanticity across architectures, activation functions or regularization.
No re-examination of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No test of how activation range or scoring choices affect polysemanticity judgments.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation (discusses) and tranche (T6) are appropriate; no verdicts are warranted. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Vision models and neuron responses to image inputs.
Whether MLP neurons in language models respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, and how prevalence varies by layer.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Whether polysemanticity prevalence changes with architecture, activation, or regularization, or can be reduced without substantial performance loss.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect one shared feature or related jobs rather than unrelated mixtures.
Whether neuron polysemanticity judgments depend on activation range or explanation-scoring choices.

rows.subject: BM1 models (CS1/CS2/CS3 variants; aggregate statement)
rows.operation_detail: Compared attention heads involved in processing table-name and field tokens in the SAE analysis.
rows.measure: Overlap between the attention heads used for table-name processing and field-token processing
rows.value: Described as a high degree of overlap; not quantified. The authors say this could indicate polysemantic heads or a similar mechanism for selecting prompt information.
rows.locator: Appendix J, paragraph preceding “Mean-Ablation Circuits”; Tables 10–12
rows.note: The paper states this qualitatively across BM1 analyses; it does not isolate individual neurons or establish that the heads respond to unrelated inputs.
rows.check: The row concerns attention heads, not MLP neurons or vision neurons. The 'overlap' is between heads important for table-name and field-token processing (Tables 10–12), which are related functions of one task, not unrelated inputs. The row is unquantified, and the authors leave its interpretation open. It is better treated as a fits_no_version observation than as a result row bearing on any version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
